The process of producing high quality solder joints is

In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
variables must be in control. The five general process 
variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
Let’s take a closer look at each. 
MATERIALS 
The materials must meet functional specifications so 
that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
solderability. 
MACHINES 
The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
to their specifications. The machines should operate 
within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
able. 
MANPOWER 
The manpower must be properly trained. All machines in 
the line require knowledgeable operators and mainte- 
nance personnel. A machine is only as good as the person 
operating it. 
METHODS 
The methods and procedures must be defined and strictly 
adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the 
shelf too long. Problems should be fully documented 
including all data that pertains to it. 
ENVIRONMENT

This includes both the environment inside and outside of 
the machines. For example, if the humidity in the solder-

absorb moisture, whichmay cause problems duringreflow .

thermal profile in the reflow oven may be affected, which 
again may cause a defect.

quality SMT soldering, the reflow process.

In order to fully understand Surface Mount Technology 
(SMT) reflow, one needs to have an understanding of 
what is being accomplished. One can take too simplistic 
a viewpoint in that all you need to do is to heat solder 
to a temperature greater than its melting point. One can 
also take too complicated a viewpoint in believing that a 
certain wavelength of infrared (IR) is required, or that a 
certain percentage of convection is required. Perhaps the 
most astute comment made on surface mount reflow was 
by an individual whom had just completed an evaluation 
of vapor phase, panel IR, and lamp IR equipment nearly 
five years ago. After coming up with virtually identical 
soldering defect results on all three types of soldering 
equipment, the following comment was made: “If you 
could hit the correct reflow profile using buckets of hot 
water, you would accomplish high quality, low defect 
solder joints.” Although the above comment was made 
in jest (hot water is not quite hot enough to reflow solder), 
there is considerable truth to what was said.

REFLOW PROFILE REQUIREMENT 
High quality, low defect soldering requires identifying 
the optimum temperature profile for reflowing the solder 
paste, and repeating over and over. Every solder joint on 
every board, needs to be heated similarily if the desired 
soldering results are to be accomplished. It does not 
matter how you apply the heat to the solder joint. What 
does matter is that the heat is applied to the solder joint 
in a controlled manner. The heating and cooling rise 
rates must be compatible with the solder paste and 
components. The amount of time that the assembly is 
exposed to certain temperatures must be defined and 
maintained. In other words, the solder reflow profile 
must first be defined and then maintained.

TYPICAL PROFILE 
A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
mary, define the profile, and hit it.

If the product temperature profile is not maintained 
within the band, a defect will occur. Chip capacitors 
may crack if the rise rate in the preheat zone is exces- 
sive. Solder spatter and solder balls may occur if drying 
is excessive or insufficient. If drying is excessive, the 
solder paste may skin over and not allow any of the 
volatiles to escape. As the temperature of the solder joint 
continues to heat, the vapor pressure increases until the 
solder joint virtually explodes as the gases escape rap- 
idly. The result is solder spatter and solder balls. If the 
preheat is insufficient, solder spatter and balls may occur 
in the reflow zone when higher heating rates occur. It is 
critical that the paste is dried at low controlled heating 
rates. In the reflow zone, insufficient heat will result in 
non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The 
joints will have a dull, rough surface finish in this case. 
Excessive heating in the reflow zone may result in burnt 
boards, damaged components, or possibly solder 
dewetting. In a dewet solder joint, the solder is reflowed 
but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead. 
DEFINE THE BAND 
The profile band needs to be defined for the given SMT 
assembly. To define this band, one should be aware of 
not only the solder paste requirements, but also any 
specific requirements of components or the circuit board 
material. The process band width is defined as the total 
deviation in temperature that can occur and yield reliable 
results. 
OVEN PERFORMANCE 
From a process standpoint, the reflow oven must be able 
to produce consistent results within the reflow profile 
band. The user should be aware of all variables that 
influence the band. These variables may be defined as 
product related and oven related. By far the most critical 
product related non-uniformity is that created by large 
mass differences on the product. Since it is easier to heat 
an area that has no components as compared with an area 
with large components, temperature differentials will 
exist on the product. Machine related non-uniformities 
such as repeatability under product load and edge-to- 
center and front-to-back product heating uniformities 
must also be considered. To achieve high quality, low 
defect soldering results, the sum of all the non-uniformi- 
ties must fall within the defined reflow profile band.

a range of temperatures all solder joints

WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF IR? ... CONVECTION? 
In SMT reflow applications, there is no such thing as 
pure convection or pure IR. The only way to achieve a 
100% convection system would be to have gas flowing 
over the product with no chamber walls. Of course this 
in not practical. To have a 100% IR system, the chamber 
would need to be operated in a vacuum. Again, this is not 
the case. However, some systems are more dominated by 
convection, while others utilize IR as the primary heat 
source. For the sake of simplicity this text will refer to a 
convection dominated machine as a convection ma- 
chine, and an IR dominate machine as an IR machine. 
CONVECTION 
Both convection and IR have their unique advantages 
and limitations. In convective systems, typically the 
temperature of the flow is close to the desired tempera- 
ture of the product in a given zone. This has the 
advantage in that the product temperature will never 
exceed the gas flow temperature. This is useful when 
heating a product that has a large difference in the mass 
of the components and distribution. In this case, the 
larger components will continue to heat, while the smaller 
components will not overheat. Convection heat transfer 
is not thermally efficient. Air (or nitrogen) has a very low 
heat capacity, which means that high volumes of flow 
may be required to transfer the heat. One way to improve 
efficiency and reduce the amount of process gas required

Reflow soldering in a nitrogen atmosphere is becoming 
a significant process consideration. The issue is really 
not the ability to reflow in nitrogen, but rather the ability 
to reflow in the absence of oxygen. Heating solder in 
the presence of oxygen will create oxides, which are 
generally non-solderable surfaces. In past days of reflow 
soldering, the solder paste consisted of aggressive enough 
fluxes to remove oxides during the reflow process. The 
future trend is moving away from strong fluxes in the 
paste. The future trends include two major process 
changes that are driving the need for reflow in nitrogen 
atmospheres; fine pitch soldering and no-clean fluxes. 
500 ppm 
FINE PITCH REFLOW SOLDERING 
Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order 
to obtain satisfactory paste print definition, the particle 
sizes of tin and lead are becoming smaller. As the 
particles become smaller, the ratio of surface area to 
volume of the particles increases. This can be shown by: 
RATIO = (n x D*) /(1/6 x n x D3) 
RATIO = 6 / D 
WHERE: 
D = Particle Diameter 
FOR THE SAME VOLUME (OR MASS) OF SOLDER, THERE IS 
GREATER SURFACE AREA WITH SMALLER PARTICLES THAN 
WITH LARGER PARTICLES. 
Thus, as particles sizes decrease, the ratio increases. 
With more available surface area in the solder paste, 
there is a greater tendency towards oxidation. Keep in 
mind that oxidation is a function of the metals involved, 
the temperatures of the metal, the exposed surface area, 
and the amount of oxygen present. The only variable 
that one can control is the amount of oxygen present. 
This can only be done through proper oven design. 
NO-CLEAN SOLDERING 
The second technology change that is driving the need 
towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning 
is creating this and other needs. No-clean soldering 
requires a tight control of the process. All of the compo- 
nents and boards must be highly solderable. The reflow 
process must not add any significant oxidation to the 
process. The fluxes used are very weak, and do not have 
aggressive oxide cleaning action. In addition, there is no 
cleaning that would remove any solder balls from the 
product. These solder balls eventually can create short 
circuits on the product if they are not removed. Reflowing 
in a high purity nitrogen environment reduces the possi- 
bility of creating solder balls. 
A good question to ask is “How pure a nitrogen environ- 
ment is required?” A recent study (4) by Colin Lea of the 
National Physics Laboratory in the United Kingdom was 
conducted to determine the affect of nitrogen purity on 
the process. The conclusions drawn in the study are

When selecting reflow equipment, it is important to take 
into consideration all aspects that may affect the process 
and production. Try to avoid becoming too focussed on 
one issue, such as populated uniformity, as it may not 
lead you to the optimum decision. The recommended 
steps in the selection process are described in the follow- 
ing paragraphs. 
DEFINE PROCESS BAND WIDTH 
The first step is to define the acceptable process profile 
band width for your SMT assemblies. Try to be as 
accurate as possible when defining the band. If the band 
is too restrictive, some aspect of production will be 
negatively affected. If the band is too loose, a defect will 
show up in the process. The band width should be 
defined as a range of temperatures ("C) that the entire 
profile must fall within. Refer to page 4 for a more 
detailed description. 
DEFINE HEATING NON-UNIFORMITIES 
The next step is to define causes of heating non-unifor- 
mities that may occur in the process. These non-unifor- 
mities are caused by mass differential, oven uniformity, 
and oven repeatability under production loading condi- 
tions. A set of tests must be conducted with the desired 
product on the oven in question. The sum of the non- 
uniformities ("C) must be less than the profile band width 
defined in the first step. Refer to page 5 for a more 
detailed description.

REVIEW CONVEYOR DESIGN 
The conveying mechanism is perhaps the most over-

RELIABILITY/SERVICEABILITY 
Once a machine is placed into service, it is critical that it 
remains operational. Evaluate the product design from a 
structural as well as a functional standpoint. Is the oven 
designed to withstand the rigors of production? Review 
the product manuals, drawings, and spare parts lists. 
Find out where the nearest servicing center is located. Is 
training available? These are the questions that must be 
asked during the selection process. 
INTERFACING REQUIREMENTS 
Conveyor and control interfacing requirements may also 
be an important selection issue. Make sure that the edge 
conveyor fixed rail justification is the same as the pick- 
and-place equipment. Ask questions about networking 
machines to a host and product flow control schemes if 
needed.

CONVECTION OVEN THERMAL CONTROL 
Convection oven thermal control requires tight control 
of two variables; temperature and flow. In order to 
maintain constant heat flux to the product, it is critical 
that both these variables are controlled. Research, Inc.’s 
MICRI-FLO XG forced convection reflow system will 
be used as an example. The temperature and flow control 
are defined specific to this system. 
CONVECTION OVEN DESCRIPTION 
Temperature control of the system must consider both 
the gas and the surrounding wall temperature. Remem- 
ber, even in a convection dominant heating system, the 
walls radiate IR energy worth about 20%-30% of the 
total heat flux of the system. The figure below shows 
the heater cavity flow diagram for the MICRI-FLO XG. 
The reflow and dryout zones each receive input gas 
(air or nitrogen) through a series of flow meters. This 
controlled flow enters a diffusion plenum behind the 
heating plenum to distribute the flow. The flow then 
enters a second plenum, where the gas is preheated by a 
series of heaters. The heaters consist of a wound nickel- 
chromium wire encased in a stainless steel jacket. The

can occur from one side of the machine. The gas then

The product is heated from a combination of the hot gas 
and the hot chamber surroundings. A control thermo- 
couple is mounted in each zone to maintain cavity 
repeatability. A PID (Proportional - Integral - Deriva-

constant conditions. 
The flow is removed from the reflow area by two exhaust 
ducts located on each side of the reflow zone. This flow 
is pulled from the zones using a high temperature, low 
flow recirculating blower. The flow is pushed by the 
blower through the preheater plenum arrangement. The 
temperature control is accomplished in the same way as 
the dryout and reflow zone. 
The flow that heats the product (in all zones) is forced 
through the walls in an array of holes to break up the 
boundary layers on the product. The perpendicular flow 
arrangement shown on page 8 is used to optimize heat 
transfer.

Convection ovens are a greater challenge to inert for 
several reasons. First, the amount of flow that would be 
required to transfer 80% of the energy by convection is 
extremely high, and cost prohibitive. In order to mini- 
mize this, recirculation ducts are added, which result in 
the degradation of the purity of the source flow entering 
a given zone. Higher velocities and turbulent flow are 
also required, which can result in a greater opportunity 
for oxygen to enter the system. Third, the pressure in the 
heater cavity is positive in some areas, and negative in 
others. Balancing this flow becomes adifficult task. The 
job of inerting a convection oven is not impossible. 
However, it should be noted that purity levels and flow 
rates are less optimum than with an IR based machine. 
CHAMBER DESCRIPTION 
Many of the same principles apply for inerting when 
comparing a convection oven to an IR oven. The MZCRZ- 
FLO XG convection oven shown below utilizes a very 
similar scheme to the 4470XN IR oven. The gas is 
brought into each zone very uniformly using the propri-

etary gas plenum distribution system. The pressure in the 
entry and exit purge sections are maintained at sufficient 
levels to minimize oxygen infiltration. Flow meter 
controlled venturi exhausts are used to balance the flow 
in the system and to remove process volatiles. 
In order to maintain the best purity levels in the zones 
where the product temperature is greater than 150°C, 
pure nitrogen is delivered to the reflow and dryout 
zone. This is a key point, as this ensures that the product 
experiences a nearly pure environment at its most criti- 
cal stages (dryout and reflow). The recirculated gas 
from these zones is reheated and used in the preheat zone. 
Here, purity is not as critical, so the use of recirculated 
gas is not detrimental to the process. 
Purity levels in the dryout and reflow zone can be 
maintained at 35 PPM over incoming purity levels at 
flow rates of 1800 cubic feet per hour (5 1 cubic meters 
per hour).

IR/CONVECTION OVEN CLOSED LOOP CONTROL 
One of the key oven performance issues is the ability to 
repeat a product temperature profile. Repeatability is 
influenced most by product loading. Heavy or non- 
variable loading can result in the oven incorrectly com- 
pensating, resulting in a loss of repeatability. High levels 
of repeatability can be achieved only if all the compo- 
nents of heat transfer are maintained constant. 
LAMP DEFINITION 
The closed loop heat flux control method used in a 
Research, Inc. lamp based oven will be used as an 
example of one type of control. The primary heat source 
in this system is the tungsten filament (T3) lamp. The T3 
lamp consists of a tungsten filament encased in a sealed 
quartz envelope. The envelope is filled with an inert gas 
to keep the filament from oxidizing and failing. The 
lamps are rated for 5000 hours when operated at 100% 
capacity. In SMT applications, the lamp power never 
exceeds 20% capacity, resulting in lamp life in excess of 
20,000 hours. At typical operating setpoints of 5-15%, 
the heat transfer to the product is controlled such that 
heating rates are under 2”C/second, and the IR emission 
is in the medium to long wavelength range. 
The greatest advantage that T3 lamps have is their rapid 
response capability. Within 1 to 2 seconds after a voltage 
change occurs, the lamp is at its new temperature equi- 
librium. This rapid response is ideal for closed loop 
control, as energy can be replaced in the heating chamber 
instantly after its removal.

Accurate contol is not achieved by maintaining only one 
of the components constant, but rather the sum of all the 
thermal energies involved. The lamp IR component is 
regulated by the SCRpower controlled system. The wall 
and convective components are collectively monitored 
by the bulk chamber temperature measured with a ther- 
mocouple probe. There are two reference setpoints; 
percent voltage for the lamp, and the bulk chamber 
temperature. The bulk chamber setpoint drives the 
equation. If the chamber is at the correct temperature, 
then the lamp setpoints will be at their setpoints. If the 
chamber is too hot, then the lamps will decrease in 
intensity. If the chamber is too cool, the lamps will 
operate at a level greater than their setpoint. The lamp 
power is modified only enough to compensate for the 
bulk chamber heat transfer deviation. In doing so, the 
total heat flux to the product is maintained. The correct 
compensation will occur providing the bulk chamber 
temperature is within k 25°C. Product temperature 
repeatability o f f  2.5”C will occur if the bulk chamber 
is within this defined band. 
The ability to operate within this wide band has two 
significant advantages. The first is that the oven may 
be loaded down to levels up to 80% load. The second is 
that profile changeover times are reduced significantly. 
Loading may begin when all oven temperatures are 
within f 25°C of setpoint. This requires far less time to 
achieve the “ready” state than if the “ready” process 
window was f 3”C, which is often the case inreflow oven 
operation. Warm-up times of less than 15 minutes occur. 
Profile changeover times are 3 to 5 minutes for profile 
increases of under 40”C, and under 10 minutes for profile 
decreases of under 40°C. Even in the worst case of going 
from a reflow profile to an adhesive cure profile, the 
changeover time is under 15 minutes.

Infrared ovens do not require high quantities of flow to

NITROGEN OVEN DESCRIPTION 
The 4470XN from Research, Inc. is an example of an IR 
dominant oven that provides a high purity nitrogen 
environment at low flow levels. 
The system uses a 
proprietary gas flow distribution method through the 
chamber walls to uniformly blanket the chamber with the 
process nitrogen. A slight positive pressure inside the 
chamber helps minimize external room effects and helps 
keep oxygen out of the chamber. Entry and exit purge 
sections are present to provide a nitrogen curtain at the 
chamber entrance and exit, which also assists in keeping 
oxygen out of the chamber. Flow meter controlled 
venturi exhausts are used to balance the flow in the 
system and to remove process volatiles. 
PREHEAT BOTTOM (IR2) 
The gas system is non-recirculatory, in that the gas is 
used once and then expended. This has the advantage 
that process contaminants are not recirculated which 
helps maintain high nitrogen purity levels. The heat 
chamber is accessible by unfastening six clamps and 
elevating the top heater vertically through the use of a 
crank mechanism. Purity levels of 20 PPM (over in- 
coming purity level) are attainable in all heating zones. 
Flow rates are in the 1200 to 1600 cubic feet per hour 
(34 to 45 cubic meters per hour) range. Machines in the 
field are experiencing total purity levels of 10-15 PPM 
(including incoming) at flow rates of 1300 cubic feet per 
hour (37 cubic meters per hour). These purity levels are 
measured with the machine fully loaded with product.

EDGE CONVEYOR 
Proper design of the edge conveying system is critical, 
as typically only 0.17 inches (4 mm) is in contact with 
the bottom side edges of the product. If the conveyor 
has lateral warpage of greater than this amount, the 
product will fall into the oven. Thus, edge conveyor 
straightness is a key issue in SMT processing. 
As the conveyor rails heat during the machine warm-up 
period, they will grow and tend to warp. The patented 
system from Research, Inc. shown below tensions the 
rails, which pulls the rail assembly straight. The lever 
(outlined in dark) is attached to the rail. The bottom side 
of the lever is attached to an adjustable spring mechanism 
that runs from end to end in the machine. Approximately 
1500 lbs (681 kg) of tensioning force is applied to each 
rail to maintain straightness. The machine frame is made 
of welded structural tubing in order to maintain its 
structural integrity. 
The use of the tensioning system allows the mass of the 
rails to be maintained at a reasonably low value, which 
minimizes the thermal affect of the rail on the product.

    78→CONTROL VARIABLES 
    79→In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
    80→variables must be in control. The five general process 
    81→variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
    82→rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
    83→ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
    84→a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
    85→Let’s take a closer look at each. 
    86→MATERIALS 
    87→The materials must meet functional specifications so 
    88→that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
    89→importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
    90→solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
    91→base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
    92→paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
    93→solderability. 
    94→MACHINES 
    95→The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
    96→to their specifications. The machines should operate 
    97→within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
    98→machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
    99→a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
   100→able.

   108→adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
   109→to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the

   113→Finally, the processing environment must be controlled.

   195→TYPICAL PROFILE 
   196→A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
   197→section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
   198→the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
   199→assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
   200→150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
   201→is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
   202→The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
   203→components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
   204→capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
   205→fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
   206→The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
   207→soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
   208→the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
   209→temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
   210→zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
   211→plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
   212→elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
   213→of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
   214→temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
   215→ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
   216→The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
   217→point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
   218→time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
   219→wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
   220→the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
   221→mary, define the profile, and hit it.

   301→If the product temperature profile is not maintained 
   302→within the band, a defect will occur. Chip capacitors 
   303→may crack if the rise rate in the preheat zone is exces- 
   304→sive. Solder spatter and solder balls may occur if drying 
   305→is excessive or insufficient. If drying is excessive, the 
   306→solder paste may skin over and not allow any of the 
   307→volatiles to escape. As the temperature of the solder joint 
   308→continues to heat, the vapor pressure increases until the 
   309→solder joint virtually explodes as the gases escape rap- 
   310→idly. The result is solder spatter and solder balls. If the 
   311→preheat is insufficient, solder spatter and balls may occur 
   312→in the reflow zone when higher heating rates occur. It is 
   313→critical that the paste is dried at low controlled heating 
   314→rates. In the reflow zone, insufficient heat will result in 
   315→non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The 
   316→joints will have a dull, rough surface finish in this case. 
   317→Excessive heating in the reflow zone may result in burnt 
   318→boards, damaged components, or possibly solder 
   319→dewetting. In a dewet solder joint, the solder is reflowed 
   320→but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead. 
   321→DEFINE THE BAND 
   322→The profile band needs to be defined for the given SMT 
   323→assembly. To define this band, one should be aware of 
   324→not only the solder paste requirements, but also any 
   325→specific requirements of components or the circuit board 
   326→material. The process band width is defined as the total 
   327→deviation in temperature that can occur and yield reliable 
   328→results. 
   329→OVEN PERFORMANCE 
   330→From a process standpoint, the reflow oven must be able 
   331→to produce consistent results within the reflow profile 
   332→band. The user should be aware of all variables that 
   333→influence the band. These variables may be defined as 
   334→product related and oven related. By far the most critical 
   335→product related non-uniformity is that created by large 
   336→mass differences on the product. Since it is easier to heat 
   337→an area that has no components as compared with an area 
   338→with large components, temperature differentials will 
   339→exist on the product. Machine related non-uniformities 
   340→such as repeatability under product load and edge-to- 
   341→center and front-to-back product heating uniformities 
   342→must also be considered. To achieve high quality, low 
   343→defect soldering results, the sum of all the non-uniformi- 
   344→ties must fall within the defined reflow profile band. 
   345→In reality the profile is not a line, but rather 
   346→a range of temperatures all solder joints 
   347→must be exposed. 
   348→The total temperature deviation from 
   349→component thermal mismatch, oven load- 
   350→ing, and oven uniformity must be within 
   351→the band.

   354→WHAT ARE THE CAUSES OF NON-UNIFORM HEATING?

   356→the defined process band, one needs to better understand 
   357→the causes of heating non-uniformities. The three main 
   358→causes of non-uniform heating in the SMT reflow pro- 
   359→cess include mass differential on the product, conveyor 
   360→and heater edge effects, and product loading.

   400→effect, similar to the one described above. The oven 
   401→uniformity may be measured by thermocoupling a bare 
   402→board over a matrix of points, and running a profile. The 
   403→matrix should include points on the board edges (front, 
   404→back, left, and right), and the center of the board.

   648→WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF IR? ... CONVECTION? 
   649→In SMT reflow applications, there is no such thing as 
   650→pure convection or pure IR. The only way to achieve a 
   651→100% convection system would be to have gas flowing 
   652→over the product with no chamber walls. Of course this 
   653→in not practical. To have a 100% IR system, the chamber 
   654→would need to be operated in a vacuum. Again, this is not 
   655→the case. However, some systems are more dominated by 
   656→convection, while others utilize IR as the primary heat 
   657→source. For the sake of simplicity this text will refer to a 
   658→convection dominated machine as a convection ma- 
   659→chine, and an IR dominate machine as an IR machine. 
   660→CONVECTION 
   661→Both convection and IR have their unique advantages 
   662→and limitations. In convective systems, typically the 
   663→temperature of the flow is close to the desired tempera- 
   664→ture of the product in a given zone. This has the 
   665→advantage in that the product temperature will never 
   666→exceed the gas flow temperature. This is useful when 
   667→heating a product that has a large difference in the mass 
   668→of the components and distribution. In this case, the 
   669→larger components will continue to heat, while the smaller 
   670→components will not overheat. Convection heat transfer 
   671→is not thermally efficient. Air (or nitrogen) has a very low 
   672→heat capacity, which means that high volumes of flow 
   673→may be required to transfer the heat. One way to improve 
   674→efficiency and reduce the amount of process gas required

   723→Reflow soldering in a nitrogen atmosphere is becoming 
   724→a significant process consideration. The issue is really 
   725→not the ability to reflow in nitrogen, but rather the ability 
   726→to reflow in the absence of oxygen. Heating solder in 
   727→the presence of oxygen will create oxides, which are 
   728→generally non-solderable surfaces. In past days of reflow 
   729→soldering, the solder paste consisted of aggressive enough 
   730→fluxes to remove oxides during the reflow process. The 
   731→future trend is moving away from strong fluxes in the 
   732→paste. The future trends include two major process 
   733→changes that are driving the need for reflow in nitrogen 
   734→atmospheres; fine pitch soldering and no-clean fluxes. 
   735→500 ppm 
   736→FINE PITCH REFLOW SOLDERING 
   737→Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order 
   738→to obtain satisfactory paste print definition, the particle 
   739→sizes of tin and lead are becoming smaller. As the 
   740→particles become smaller, the ratio of surface area to 
   741→volume of the particles increases. This can be shown by: 
   742→RATIO = (n x D*) /(1/6 x n x D3) 
   743→RATIO = 6 / D 
   744→WHERE: 
   745→D = Particle Diameter 
   746→FOR THE SAME VOLUME (OR MASS) OF SOLDER, THERE IS 
   747→GREATER SURFACE AREA WITH SMALLER PARTICLES THAN 
   748→WITH LARGER PARTICLES. 
   749→Thus, as particles sizes decrease, the ratio increases. 
   750→With more available surface area in the solder paste, 
   751→there is a greater tendency towards oxidation. Keep in 
   752→mind that oxidation is a function of the metals involved, 
   753→the temperatures of the metal, the exposed surface area, 
   754→and the amount of oxygen present. The only variable 
   755→that one can control is the amount of oxygen present. 
   756→This can only be done through proper oven design. 
   757→NO-CLEAN SOLDERING 
   758→The second technology change that is driving the need 
   759→towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
   760→clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning 
   761→is creating this and other needs. No-clean soldering 
   762→requires a tight control of the process. All of the compo- 
   763→nents and boards must be highly solderable. The reflow 
   764→process must not add any significant oxidation to the 
   765→process. The fluxes used are very weak, and do not have 
   766→aggressive oxide cleaning action. In addition, there is no 
   767→cleaning that would remove any solder balls from the 
   768→product. These solder balls eventually can create short 
   769→circuits on the product if they are not removed. Reflowing 
   770→in a high purity nitrogen environment reduces the possi- 
   771→bility of creating solder balls.

   773→ment is required?” A recent study (4) by Colin Lea of the

   803→WHAT ARE THE STEPS IN THE SELECTION PROCESS? 
   804→When selecting reflow equipment, it is important to take 
   805→into consideration all aspects that may affect the process 
   806→and production. Try to avoid becoming too focussed on 
   807→one issue, such as populated uniformity, as it may not 
   808→lead you to the optimum decision. The recommended 
   809→steps in the selection process are described in the follow- 
   810→ing paragraphs. 
   811→DEFINE PROCESS BAND WIDTH 
   812→The first step is to define the acceptable process profile 
   813→band width for your SMT assemblies. Try to be as 
   814→accurate as possible when defining the band. If the band 
   815→is too restrictive, some aspect of production will be 
   816→negatively affected. If the band is too loose, a defect will 
   817→show up in the process. The band width should be 
   818→defined as a range of temperatures ("C) that the entire 
   819→profile must fall within. Refer to page 4 for a more 
   820→detailed description. 
   821→DEFINE HEATING NON-UNIFORMITIES 
   822→The next step is to define causes of heating non-unifor- 
   823→mities that may occur in the process. These non-unifor- 
   824→mities are caused by mass differential, oven uniformity, 
   825→and oven repeatability under production loading condi- 
   826→tions. A set of tests must be conducted with the desired 
   827→product on the oven in question. The sum of the non- 
   828→uniformities ("C) must be less than the profile band width

  1020→CONVECTION OVEN THERMAL CONTROL 
  1021→Convection oven thermal control requires tight control 
  1022→of two variables; temperature and flow. In order to 
  1023→maintain constant heat flux to the product, it is critical 
  1024→that both these variables are controlled. Research, Inc.’s 
  1025→MICRI-FLO XG forced convection reflow system will 
  1026→be used as an example. The temperature and flow control 
  1027→are defined specific to this system. 
  1028→CONVECTION OVEN DESCRIPTION 
  1029→Temperature control of the system must consider both 
  1030→the gas and the surrounding wall temperature. Remem- 
  1031→ber, even in a convection dominant heating system, the 
  1032→walls radiate IR energy worth about 20%-30% of the 
  1033→total heat flux of the system. The figure below shows 
  1034→the heater cavity flow diagram for the MICRI-FLO XG. 
  1035→The reflow and dryout zones each receive input gas 
  1036→(air or nitrogen) through a series of flow meters. This 
  1037→controlled flow enters a diffusion plenum behind the 
  1038→heating plenum to distribute the flow. The flow then 
  1039→enters a second plenum, where the gas is preheated by a 
  1040→series of heaters. The heaters consist of a wound nickel- 
  1041→chromium wire encased in a stainless steel jacket. The

  1051→The product is heated from a combination of the hot gas

  1076→CONVECTION OVEN WITH 
  1077→Convection ovens are a greater challenge to inert for 
  1078→several reasons. First, the amount of flow that would be 
  1079→required to transfer 80% of the energy by convection is 
  1080→extremely high, and cost prohibitive. In order to mini- 
  1081→mize this, recirculation ducts are added, which result in 
  1082→the degradation of the purity of the source flow entering 
  1083→a given zone. Higher velocities and turbulent flow are 
  1084→also required, which can result in a greater opportunity 
  1085→for oxygen to enter the system. Third, the pressure in the 
  1086→heater cavity is positive in some areas, and negative in 
  1087→others. Balancing this flow becomes adifficult task. The 
  1088→job of inerting a convection oven is not impossible. 
  1089→However, it should be noted that purity levels and flow 
  1090→rates are less optimum than with an IR based machine. 
  1091→CHAMBER DESCRIPTION 
  1092→Many of the same principles apply for inerting when 
  1093→comparing a convection oven to an IR oven. The MZCRZ- 
  1094→FLO XG convection oven shown below utilizes a very 
  1095→similar scheme to the 4470XN IR oven. The gas is 
  1096→brought into each zone very uniformly using the propri- 
  1097→VITROGEN ATMOSPHERE 
  1098→etary gas plenum distribution system. The pressure in the 
  1099→entry and exit purge sections are maintained at sufficient 
  1100→levels to minimize oxygen infiltration. Flow meter 
  1101→controlled venturi exhausts are used to balance the flow 
  1102→in the system and to remove process volatiles. 
  1103→In order to maintain the best purity levels in the zones 
  1104→where the product temperature is greater than 150°C, 
  1105→pure nitrogen is delivered to the reflow and dryout

  1110→Here, purity is not as critical, so the use of recirculated 
  1111→gas is not detrimental to the process. 
  1112→Purity levels in the dryout and reflow zone can be

  1126→IR/CONVECTION OVEN CLOSED LOOP CONTROL 
  1127→One of the key oven performance issues is the ability to 
  1128→repeat a product temperature profile. Repeatability is 
  1129→influenced most by product loading. Heavy or non- 
  1130→variable loading can result in the oven incorrectly com- 
  1131→pensating, resulting in a loss of repeatability. High levels 
  1132→of repeatability can be achieved only if all the compo- 
  1133→nents of heat transfer are maintained constant. 
  1134→LAMP DEFINITION 
  1135→The closed loop heat flux control method used in a 
  1136→Research, Inc. lamp based oven will be used as an 
  1137→example of one type of control. The primary heat source 
  1138→in this system is the tungsten filament (T3) lamp. The T3 
  1139→lamp consists of a tungsten filament encased in a sealed 
  1140→quartz envelope. The envelope is filled with an inert gas 
  1141→to keep the filament from oxidizing and failing. The 
  1142→lamps are rated for 5000 hours when operated at 100% 
  1143→capacity. In SMT applications, the lamp power never 
  1144→exceeds 20% capacity, resulting in lamp life in excess of 
  1145→20,000 hours. At typical operating setpoints of 5-15%, 
  1146→the heat transfer to the product is controlled such that 
  1147→heating rates are under 2”C/second, and the IR emission 
  1148→is in the medium to long wavelength range. 
  1149→The greatest advantage that T3 lamps have is their rapid 
  1150→response capability. Within 1 to 2 seconds after a voltage 
  1151→change occurs, the lamp is at its new temperature equi- 
  1152→librium. This rapid response is ideal for closed loop 
  1153→control, as energy can be replaced in the heating chamber 
  1154→instantly after its removal. 
  1155→CONTROL DEFINITION 
  1156→In order for the product profile to be repeatable, the total 
  1157→heat flux to the product must be held constant. The total 
  1158→heat flux to the product is the sum of IR from the lamp and 
  1159→wall plus the convective component. Refer to the figure. 
  1160→Within 1 to 2 seconds after a voltage change 
  1161→occurs, the lamp is at its new temperature 
  1162→equilibrium. This rapid response is ideal for 
  1163→closed loop control, as energy can be replaced 
  1164→in the heating chamber instantly after its

  1177→Accurate contol is not achieved by maintaining only one

  1180→regulated by the SCRpower controlled system. The wall

  1183→mocouple probe. There are two reference setpoints; 
  1184→percent voltage for the lamp, and the bulk chamber 
  1185→temperature. The bulk chamber setpoint drives the 
  1186→equation. If the chamber is at the correct temperature, 
  1187→then the lamp setpoints will be at their setpoints. If the 
  1188→chamber is too hot, then the lamps will decrease in 
  1189→intensity. If the chamber is too cool, the lamps will 
  1190→operate at a level greater than their setpoint. The lamp 
  1191→power is modified only enough to compensate for the 
  1192→bulk chamber heat transfer deviation. In doing so, the 
  1193→total heat flux to the product is maintained. The correct 
  1194→compensation will occur providing the bulk chamber 
  1195→temperature is within k 25°C. Product temperature 
  1196→repeatability o f f  2.5”C will occur if the bulk chamber 
  1197→is within this defined band. 
  1198→The ability to operate within this wide band has two 
  1199→significant advantages. The first is that the oven may 
  1200→be loaded down to levels up to 80% load. The second is 
  1201→that profile changeover times are reduced significantly. 
  1202→Loading may begin when all oven temperatures are 
  1203→within f 25°C of setpoint. This requires far less time to 
  1204→achieve the “ready” state than if the “ready” process 
  1205→window was f 3”C, which is often the case inreflow oven 
  1206→operation. Warm-up times of less than 15 minutes occur. 
  1207→Profile changeover times are 3 to 5 minutes for profile 
  1208→increases of under 40”C, and under 10 minutes for profile 
  1209→decreases of under 40°C. Even in the worst case of going 
  1210→from a reflow profile to an adhesive cure profile, the 
  1211→changeover time is under 15 minutes.

  1230→NITROGEN OVEN DESCRIPTION 
  1231→The 4470XN from Research, Inc. is an example of an IR 
  1232→dominant oven that provides a high purity nitrogen 
  1233→environment at low flow levels. 
  1234→The system uses a 
  1235→proprietary gas flow distribution method through the 
  1236→chamber walls to uniformly blanket the chamber with the 
  1237→process nitrogen. A slight positive pressure inside the 
  1238→chamber helps minimize external room effects and helps 
  1239→keep oxygen out of the chamber. Entry and exit purge 
  1240→sections are present to provide a nitrogen curtain at the 
  1241→chamber entrance and exit, which also assists in keeping 
  1242→oxygen out of the chamber. Flow meter controlled 
  1243→venturi exhausts are used to balance the flow in the 
  1244→system and to remove process volatiles. 
  1245→PREHEAT BOTTOM (IR2) 
  1246→The gas system is non-recirculatory, in that the gas is 
  1247→used once and then expended. This has the advantage 
  1248→that process contaminants are not recirculated which 
  1249→helps maintain high nitrogen purity levels. The heat 
  1250→chamber is accessible by unfastening six clamps and 
  1251→elevating the top heater vertically through the use of a 
  1252→crank mechanism. Purity levels of 20 PPM (over in- 
  1253→coming purity level) are attainable in all heating zones. 
  1254→Flow rates are in the 1200 to 1600 cubic feet per hour 
  1255→(34 to 45 cubic meters per hour) range. Machines in the 
  1256→field are experiencing total purity levels of 10-15 PPM 
  1257→(including incoming) at flow rates of 1300 cubic feet per 
  1258→hour (37 cubic meters per hour). These purity levels are 
  1259→measured with the machine fully loaded with product.

  1275→EDGE CONVEYOR 
  1276→Proper design of the edge conveying system is critical, 
  1277→as typically only 0.17 inches (4 mm) is in contact with 
  1278→the bottom side edges of the product. If the conveyor 
  1279→has lateral warpage of greater than this amount, the 
  1280→product will fall into the oven. Thus, edge conveyor 
  1281→straightness is a key issue in SMT processing. 
  1282→As the conveyor rails heat during the machine warm-up 
  1283→period, they will grow and tend to warp. The patented 
  1284→system from Research, Inc. shown below tensions the 
  1285→rails, which pulls the rail assembly straight. The lever 
  1286→(outlined in dark) is attached to the rail. The bottom side 
  1287→of the lever is attached to an adjustable spring mechanism 
  1288→that runs from end to end in the machine. Approximately 
  1289→1500 lbs (681 kg) of tensioning force is applied to each 
  1290→rail to maintain straightness. The machine frame is made 
  1291→of welded structural tubing in order to maintain its 
  1292→structural integrity. 
  1293→The use of the tensioning system allows the mass of the 
  1294→rails to be maintained at a reasonably low value, which 
  1295→minimizes the thermal affect of the rail on the product.

HOW DO YOU ACHIEVE HIGH QUALITY SOLDER JOINTS? 
The process of producing high quality solder joints is 
similar to the process of learning how to ride a bicycle. 
If you do not understand the fundamentals, it is virtually 
impossible. However, once you understand and imple- 
ment the basics, the results will follow. The goal of all 
SMT process engineers is to repeatedly produce high 
quality solder joints that have fine grain structure and 
excellent wetting characteristics, as shown in the figure 
below: 
SURFACES MUST BE 
CLEAN AND SOLDERABLE 
II 
MUST BE 
1 
SMALL 
CONTROL VARIABLES 
In order to produce high quality solderjoints, all process 
variables must be in control. The five general process 
variables (l) that need to be in control include the mate- 
rials, machines, manpower, methods, and the environ- 
ment. If the process variables are not in control, there is 
a very good chance that soldering defects will exist. 
Let’s take a closer look at each. 
MATERIALS 
The materials must meet functional specifications so 
that the product will perform to specification. Of equal 
importance is the solderability of the assembly. The 
solder paste/flux system must be compatible with the 
base materials of the parts to be soldered. The solder 
paste and parts should be as fresh as possible to enhance 
solderability. 
MACHINES 
The machines used in the process must be able to perform 
to their specifications. The machines should operate 
within the range for which they are designed. Pushing a 
machine beyond its operating limits will ultimately cause 
a problem. The machines must be reliable and service- 
able. 
MANPOWER 
The manpower must be properly trained. All machines in 
the line require knowledgeable operators and mainte- 
nance personnel. A machine is only as good as the person 
operating it. 
METHODS 
The methods and procedures must be defined and strictly 
adhered to. Inventory procedures should be implemented 
to ensure that components and boards do not stay on the 
shelf too long. Problems should be fully documented 
including all data that pertains to it. 
ENVIRONMENT 
Finally, the processing environment must be controlled. 
This includes both the environment inside and outside of 
the machines. For example, if the humidity in the solder- 
ing area is too high, this can cause the solder paste to 
absorb moisture, whichmay cause problems duringreflow . 
If the temperature in the room is not controlled, the 
thermal profile in the reflow oven may be affected, which 
again may cause a defect. 
The purpose of this text is to address one aspect of high 
quality SMT soldering, the reflow process. 
Producing high quality solder joints 
requires that five general process 
variables need to be in control; the 
materials, machines, manpower, 
methods, and the environment. 
2 
Section I - Technology 
WHAT IS THE IMPORTANCE OF THE PROFILE?

In order to fully understand Surface Mount Technology 
(SMT) reflow, one needs to have an understanding of 
what is being accomplished. One can take too simplistic 
a viewpoint in that all you need to do is to heat solder 
to a temperature greater than its melting point. One can 
also take too complicated a viewpoint in believing that a 
certain wavelength of infrared (IR) is required, or that a 
certain percentage of convection is required. Perhaps the 
most astute comment made on surface mount reflow was 
by an individual whom had just completed an evaluation 
of vapor phase, panel IR, and lamp IR equipment nearly 
five years ago. After coming up with virtually identical 
soldering defect results on all three types of soldering 
equipment, the following comment was made: “If you 
could hit the correct reflow profile using buckets of hot 
water, you would accomplish high quality, low defect 
solder joints.” Although the above comment was made 
in jest (hot water is not quite hot enough to reflow solder), 
there is considerable truth to what was said. 
I 
REFLOW PROFILE REQUIREMENT 
High quality, low defect soldering requires identifying 
the optimum temperature profile for reflowing the solder 
paste, and repeating over and over. Every solder joint on 
every board, needs to be heated similarily if the desired 
soldering results are to be accomplished. It does not 
matter how you apply the heat to the solder joint. What 
does matter is that the heat is applied to the solder joint 
in a controlled manner. The heating and cooling rise 
rates must be compatible with the solder paste and 
components. The amount of time that the assembly is 
exposed to certain temperatures must be defined and 
maintained. In other words, the solder reflow profile 
must first be defined and then maintained.

TYPICAL PROFILE 
A typical profile consists of a preheat, dryout, and reflow 
section (zone) where different heating rates are used. In 
the preheat section, the goal is to fully preheat the SMT 
assembly to temperatures generally between 100°C to 
150°C. The most critical parameter in the preheat section 
is to minimize the rate of rise to less than 2”C/second. 
The main concern is minimizing thermal shock on the 
components of the assembly. Multilayer ceramic chip 
capacitors can be vulnerable to cracking if heated too 
fast. Solder paste can spatter also, if heated too fast. 
The second heating section, referred to as the dryout, 
soak, or preflow zone, is used primarily to ensure that 
the solder paste is fully dried before hitting reflow 
temperatures. This zone also acts as a flux activation 
zone for some solder pastes. Solder reflow is accom- 
plished in the reflow zone, where the solder paste is 
elevated to a temperature greater than the melting point 
of the solder. For 63/37 Eutectic solder, the melting 
temperature is 183°C. This temperature must be ex- 
ceeded by approximately 20°C to ensure quality reflow. 
The amount of time the solder joint is above the melting 
point is referred to as the “wetting time”. The wetting 
time is normally 30 to 60 seconds for most pastes. If the 
wetting time is excessive, intermetallics may occur in 
the joint, which result in brittle solder joints. In sum- 
mary, define the profile, and hit it. 
Section I - Technology 
3 
HOW MANY HEATING ZONES ARE REQUIRED? 
This question frequently arrives and can be a source of 
confusion. One theory is that if ten zones are good, then 
twenty zones are better. While in theory this may be true, 
in practicality it may not be true. While it improves the 
flexibility of oven, it also adds to the complexity and 
makes oven set-up more difficult. 
Let’s review this question from the standpoint of how 
many zones are really needed. Reflowing solder paste 
typically requires two or three different heating rates to 
accomplish the process. In the figure below, there are 
three “typical” profile bands for RMA, water soluble, 
and no-clean solder pastes. These profiles are rather 
generic, and one should consult with their solder paste 
vendor to determine the desired profile. All of the pastes 
in the figure could be successfully reflowed using 
three zones. 
reflow is that if you can control your top and bottom 
heaters separately, then double sided reflow can be 
accomplished (without reflowing side A twice). This 
will not work with most SMT reflow processes, as most 
products are too thermally thin. Independent topbottom 
heating control does help in machines with dual convey- 
ors that are located at different heights in the chamber. 
Product warpage may also be minimized through proper 
control. The bottom line is that most machines have this 
feature, but most often the top and bottom heaters will be 
set at the same value. 
Edge heating zones become significant when edge con- 
veyors are used. Edge conveyors act as heat sinks on the 
edge of the product. Two zones of edge heat (one front, 
one back) will assist in compensating for edge con- 
veyors. If mesh conveyors are used, these zones are 
unnecessary unless the product width is quite wide. 
A second issue is the question of independent top and 
bottom heat control. A common conception in SMT

Section I - Technology 
WHAT IS THE PROFILE PROCESS BAND? 
In reality the profile is not a line, but rather a band or 
process window.(*) The size of the band is defined by the 
range of temperature deviation that can occur during 
reflow and yield high quality results. This is indicated 
by the crosshatched area shown in the figure. In the 
example, the profile band size is indicated as 25°C. 
The actual size of the band will vary depending upon 
solder paste, component type, and circuit board material.

REFLOW SOLDERING DEFECTS 
If the product temperature profile is not maintained 
within the band, a defect will occur. Chip capacitors 
may crack if the rise rate in the preheat zone is exces- 
sive. Solder spatter and solder balls may occur if drying 
is excessive or insufficient. If drying is excessive, the 
solder paste may skin over and not allow any of the 
volatiles to escape. As the temperature of the solder joint 
continues to heat, the vapor pressure increases until the 
solder joint virtually explodes as the gases escape rap- 
idly. The result is solder spatter and solder balls. If the 
preheat is insufficient, solder spatter and balls may occur 
in the reflow zone when higher heating rates occur. It is 
critical that the paste is dried at low controlled heating 
rates. In the reflow zone, insufficient heat will result in 
non-reflowed or partially reflowed solder joints. The 
joints will have a dull, rough surface finish in this case. 
Excessive heating in the reflow zone may result in burnt 
boards, damaged components, or possibly solder 
dewetting. In a dewet solder joint, the solder is reflowed 
but it is pulled away from the pad or the component lead. 
DEFINE THE BAND 
The profile band needs to be defined for the given SMT 
assembly. To define this band, one should be aware of 
not only the solder paste requirements, but also any 
specific requirements of components or the circuit board 
material. The process band width is defined as the total 
deviation in temperature that can occur and yield reliable 
results. 
OVEN PERFORMANCE 
From a process standpoint, the reflow oven must be able 
to produce consistent results within the reflow profile 
band. The user should be aware of all variables that 
influence the band. These variables may be defined as 
product related and oven related. By far the most critical 
product related non-uniformity is that created by large 
mass differences on the product. Since it is easier to heat 
an area that has no components as compared with an area 
with large components, temperature differentials will 
exist on the product. Machine related non-uniformities 
such as repeatability under product load and edge-to- 
center and front-to-back product heating uniformities 
must also be considered. To achieve high quality, low 
defect soldering results, the sum of all the non-uniformi- 
ties must fall within the defined reflow profile band. 
In reality the profile is not a line, but rather 
a range of temperatures all solder joints 
must be exposed. 
The total temperature deviation from 
component thermal mismatch, oven load- 
ing, and oven uniformity must be within 
the band. 
Section I - Technology 
5 
WHAT ARE THE CAUSES OF NON-UNIFORM HEATING? 
In order to fully comprehend the capability to heat within 
the defined process band, one needs to better understand 
the causes of heating non-uniformities. The three main 
causes of non-uniform heating in the SMT reflow pro- 
cess include mass differential on the product, conveyor 
and heater edge effects, and product loading. 
MASS DIFFERENTIAL 
The amount of temperature rise of a product as it travels 
through a heating zone depends upon a number of 
variables. The temperature rise of an object subjected to 
heat is determined by the following equation: 
AT = Q x A X  t / (M x Cp) 
WHERE: 
AT = Product Temperature Rise (“C) 
Q = Heat Absorbed (w/cmz) 
A = Exposed Area (cm2) 
t = Heating Dwell Time (seconds) 
M = Mass of Object (kg) 
Cp = Specific Heat (w-sec/kg-”C) 
The mass (M) times the specific heat (Cp) is often referred 
to as thermal mass. Greater thermal mass requires more 
heat to achieve a given temperature rise. In the figure 
shown below, the area populated with the PLCC’s has 
considerably more thermal mass per unit area than the 
area with the discrete components. This area will be more 
difficult to heat. The non-uniformity caused by thermal 
mass differential may be measured by thermocoupling a 
lead on the largest and smallest device, and running a 
profile.

OVEN UNIFORMITY 
A second main cause of non-uniform product heating is 
the oven heating pattern. This can be caused by edge 
effects on the heaters (less heat at the end) or by heat 
sinking of the conveyor system. The edge effect may be 
caused by insufficient airflow around the edges of the 
machine, or by non-uniformities that are inherent in the 
heaters. The heat sinking of the conveyor is really amass 
effect, similar to the one described above. The oven 
uniformity may be measured by thermocoupling a bare 
board over a matrix of points, and running a profile. The 
matrix should include points on the board edges (front, 
back, left, and right), and the center of the board. 
OVEN REPEATABILITY 
Repeatability refers to the oven’s capability to repeat a 
given profile. Repeatability is affected by machine 
loading. The figure below shows a typical product 
loading condition. The “Loading Factor” is defined in 
the figure.

The higher the value of the loading factor, the more 
difficult it is for any oven to give repeatable results. 
Ovens will generally specify a maximum loading factor 
(ranging from 0.5 to 0.9). The loading factor becomes an 
important consideration when sizing an oven. The non- 
uniformity caused by repeatability can be measured by 
running a profile on a test board, then load the oven 
down. Periodically, run the test board within the oven 
load and compare with the unloaded profile. 
The three main causes of non-uniform heating in 
the SMT reflow process include mass differential 
on the product, conveyor and heater edge effects, 
and product loading.

Section I - Technology 
WHAT ARE THE MODES OF HEATING? 
There are three different heating modes involved wit 
most SMT reflow processes; convection, conductior 
and infrared radiation (IR). All three of these heatin 
modes occur naturally in our daily lives. Perhaps th 
easiest way to understand each of these heating mode 
is through example. 
CONVECTION 
Convection heat transfer occurs when a fluid (such a 
air, nitrogen, or water) passes over a solid (such as a 
SMT assembly). A cool breeze on a hot sunny da 
provides convective cooling. Hot air from a hair drye 
provides convective heating. Convection heating c 
cooling requires contact of the flow with the solid par

Referring to a system as 100% convection or 
100% IR is incorrect. A system may be dominated

Infrared Radiation (IR) occurs when two bodies of dif- 
ferent temperature are in sight of each other. The best 
example of IR is the heating of the earth by the sun. IR 
is a non-contact heat transfer. 
RADIATION I 
In SMT reflow applications (with the exception of vapor 
phase), convection, conduction, and IR all play a role in 
the heating process. Referring to a system as 100% 
convection or 100% IR is incorrect. A system may be 
dominated by convection or IR, but the other heat trans- 
fer is always present. IR dominant systems usually range 
in the convection/IR ratio of 60/40 to 40/60. Convection 
dominant systems have ratios in the range of 70/30 to 
80/20. Conduction heat transfer occurs more within the 
product during the heating process. Heat is transferred 
through the product to help minimize hot or cold spots. 
Section I - Technology

HOW DOES INFRARED HEATING WORK? 
95.38 
Infrared (IR) heat transfer occurs when two objects at 
different temperatures are in sight of each other. The 
heat is transferred by electromagnetic waves of 0.78- 
1000 micron wavelengths. All objects emit some level 
of infrared. The quantity of infrared energy emitted and 
the wavelength of the emission are both dependent upon 
the absolute temperature of the object. As the source 
temperature increases, the heat transfer output increases 
exponentially to the fourth power. Increasing the source 
temperature results in shorter wavelengths. Decreasing 
the source temperature results in longer wavelengths. In 
SMT reflow the amount of heat transfer is important, so 
as not to exceed the 2OC/sec rate. When operating at 
these low heating rates all types of radiant emitters 
(lamps, panels, tubes) operate in the medium to long 
wavelength ranges.

HOW DOES CONVECTION HEATING WORK? 
Convection heat transfer occurs when a fluid at a given 
temperature contacts a solid mass at a different tempera- 
ture. If the fluid is hotter than the mass, the mass will be 
heated. If the fluid is cooler than the mass, the mass will 
be cooled. Perhaps the easiest way to understand convec- 
tion is to look at the convection equation and note what 
is important and what is not important. 
CONVECTION EQUATION 
The following is the general equation for convection 
heating or cooling: 
Q = H x A T

fluid and object (“C) 
The amount of heat transfer “Q’ can be modified by 
either changing the convective coefficient “H’ or the 
temperature difference “AT”. Increasing the source 
temperature will increase the temperature difference, 
and thus the amount of heat transfer “Q’ will increase 
proportionally. 
The convective coefficient “H’ can have a significant 
impact on the heat transfer “Q”. The value of “H” is 
related to a number of variables, including velocity of 
the flow and angle of attack of the flow. 
Increasing the flow velocity will increase the value of 
“H”. For example, when one is outside in the wind, a 
low velocity cool breeze on a warm day will feel quite 
nice. However, a strong wind on that same day may feel

a higher convective coefficient, and thus removes heat 
more effectively from your skin. In SMT reflow appli- 
cations, increasing the velocity of the flow also improves 
the amount of convection heat transfer. There are prac- 
tical limits to this, as too high of velocity may cause 
components to shift around. The flow direction also has 
a significant impact on “Q’. Parallel flow convection

WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF IR? ... CONVECTION? 
In SMT reflow applications, there is no such thing as 
pure convection or pure IR. The only way to achieve a 
100% convection system would be to have gas flowing 
over the product with no chamber walls. Of course this 
in not practical. To have a 100% IR system, the chamber 
would need to be operated in a vacuum. Again, this is not 
the case. However, some systems are more dominated by 
convection, while others utilize IR as the primary heat 
source. For the sake of simplicity this text will refer to a 
convection dominated machine as a convection ma- 
chine, and an IR dominate machine as an IR machine. 
CONVECTION 
Both convection and IR have their unique advantages 
and limitations. In convective systems, typically the 
temperature of the flow is close to the desired tempera- 
ture of the product in a given zone. This has the 
advantage in that the product temperature will never 
exceed the gas flow temperature. This is useful when 
heating a product that has a large difference in the mass 
of the components and distribution. In this case, the 
larger components will continue to heat, while the smaller 
components will not overheat. Convection heat transfer 
is not thermally efficient. Air (or nitrogen) has a very low 
heat capacity, which means that high volumes of flow 
may be required to transfer the heat. One way to improve 
efficiency and reduce the amount of process gas required

is through the use of recirculation. In a recirculation 
loop, the process gas from a zone is evacuated, then 
reheated and re-input into the heating chamber. The 
limitation to recirculating is that high nitrogen purity 
levels are not typically attainable. There is also a concern 
that if the gas is recirculated excessively, it may affect 
soldering quality, as the atmosphere surrounding the 
product becomes contaminated with process by-prod- 
ucts. Convection increases the chance of solder wicking, 
as typically the lead is heated faster than the circuit board. 
IR 
IR systems have the distinct advantage of high heating 
efficiencies and low process gas flows required to reflow 
solder. IR systems are normally very repeatable, and 
have the capability to transfer high quantities of heat as 
needed. This becomes quite useful when reflowing very 
dense SMT assemblies or very heavy boards. The 
limitation with IR is that a high temperature differential 
between the source and the product is required to transfer 
the heat. Products with high component mass differen- 
tial do not heat uniformly. They must be run quite slowly 
to accomplish reflow. IR systems are successful at 
reflowing products with component sizes up to and 
including 84 pin PLCC’s. Large connectors and pin grid 
arrays are quite difficult to reflow on an IR dominated 
system.

Reflow soldering in a nitrogen atmosphere is becoming 
a significant process consideration. The issue is really 
not the ability to reflow in nitrogen, but rather the ability 
to reflow in the absence of oxygen. Heating solder in 
the presence of oxygen will create oxides, which are 
generally non-solderable surfaces. In past days of reflow 
soldering, the solder paste consisted of aggressive enough 
fluxes to remove oxides during the reflow process. The 
future trend is moving away from strong fluxes in the 
paste. The future trends include two major process 
changes that are driving the need for reflow in nitrogen 
atmospheres; fine pitch soldering and no-clean fluxes.

FINE PITCH REFLOW SOLDERING 
Fine pitch soldering presents many challenges. In order 
to obtain satisfactory paste print definition, the particle 
sizes of tin and lead are becoming smaller. As the 
particles become smaller, the ratio of surface area to 
volume of the particles increases. This can be shown by: 
RATIO = (n x D*) /(1/6 x n x D3) 
RATIO = 6 / D 
WHERE: 
D = Particle Diameter 
FOR THE SAME VOLUME (OR MASS) OF SOLDER, THERE IS 
GREATER SURFACE AREA WITH SMALLER PARTICLES THAN 
WITH LARGER PARTICLES. 
Thus, as particles sizes decrease, the ratio increases. 
With more available surface area in the solder paste, 
there is a greater tendency towards oxidation. Keep in 
mind that oxidation is a function of the metals involved, 
the temperatures of the metal, the exposed surface area, 
and the amount of oxygen present. The only variable 
that one can control is the amount of oxygen present. 
This can only be done through proper oven design. 
NO-CLEAN SOLDERING 
The second technology change that is driving the need 
towards nitrogen atmospheres is the greater usage of no- 
clean pastes. The rapid trend away from solvent cleaning 
is creating this and other needs. No-clean soldering 
requires a tight control of the process. All of the compo- 
nents and boards must be highly solderable. The reflow 
process must not add any significant oxidation to the 
process. The fluxes used are very weak, and do not have 
aggressive oxide cleaning action. In addition, there is no 
cleaning that would remove any solder balls from the 
product. These solder balls eventually can create short 
circuits on the product if they are not removed. Reflowing 
in a high purity nitrogen environment reduces the possi- 
bility of creating solder balls.

ment is required?” A recent study (4) by Colin Lea of the

I now have the handbook text. Let me extract the key definitions and requirements:

**From the handbook:**

1. **Preheat section**: Temperature generally between 100°C to 150°C. The most critical parameter is to **minimize the rate of rise to less than 2°C/second** (page 3, line 201).

2. **Wetting time (Time Above Liquidus - TAL)**: Normally **30 to 60 seconds** for most pastes (page 3, line 218).

3. **Reflow temperature**: For 63/37 Eutectic solder, melting temperature is 183°C. Must be exceeded by approximately **20°C** to ensure quality reflow (page 3, lines 213-215).

4. **Peak temperature requirement**: From the formula on page 3 line 215, peak temperature should be approximately **20°C above the melting point** (liquidus temperature).

5. **Thermocouple measurement**: The handbook mentions thermocoupling "a lead on the largest and smallest device" (page 6, lines 381-383). The "largest_mass" thermocouple would be the most representative for preheat ramp rate (as it's the most vulnerable to cracking if heated too fast).

6. **Conveyor speed and dwell time**: The process speed is calculated as:
   - `PROCESS_SPEED = OVEN_CHAMBER_HEATED_LENGTH / PROCESS_DWELL_TIME` (page 12, lines 851-853)
   - `LINE_SPEED_MIN = BOARDS_PER_MINUTE × LENGTH_PER_BOARD / LOAD_FACTOR` (page 12, lines 835-837)

    df = df.sort_values('time_s')
    temps = df['temp_c'].values
    times = df['time_s'].values

    ramp_rates = []
    for i in range(1, len(temps)):
        dt = times[i] - times[i-1]
        if dt > 0:
            dtemp = temps[i] - temps[i-1]
            ramp_rate = dtemp / dt
            # Only consider preheat zone (100-150°C)
            # We look at the temperature at the start of the interval
            if PREHEAT_MIN_C <= temps[i-1] <= PREHEAT_MAX_C:
                ramp_rates.append(ramp_rate)
    return ramp_rates

all_runs = mes_df['run_id'].unique()
tc_runs = tc_df['run_id'].unique()

# The largest_mass thermocouple is the most representative for preheat ramp rate
# because it represents the most vulnerable component to thermal shock

max_ramp_by_run = {}
violating_runs = []

    run_tc_data = tc_df[tc_df['run_id'] == run_id]

        max_ramp_by_run[run_id] = {

            "max_preheat_ramp_c_per_s": None

        continue

    largest_mass_tc = None

        if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray):

            if PREHEAT_MIN_C <= temps[i-1] <= PREHEAT_MAX_C:
                ramp_rates.append(ramp_rate)
    return ramp_rates

# Get all runs from MES
all_runs = mes_df['run_id'].unique()
tc_runs = tc_df['run_id'].unique()

# Handbook says to use the "largest mass" thermocouple for measuring thermal mass differential
# The largest_mass thermocouple is the most representative for preheat ramp rate
# because it represents the most vulnerable component to thermal shock

max_ramp_by_run = {}
violating_runs = []

for run_id in sorted(all_runs):
    run_tc_data = tc_df[tc_df['run_id'] == run_id]

    if run_tc_data.empty:
        # No thermocouple data for this run
        max_ramp_by_run[run_id] = {

        }
        continue

    # Get thermocouples for this run
    tc_ids = run_tc_data['tc_id'].unique()

    # Per handbook, use largest_mass thermocouple as most representative
    # (it's the most vulnerable to cracking from fast heating)
    largest_mass_tc = None
    for tc_id in tc_ids:
        tc_data = run_tc_data[run_tc_data['tc_id'] == tc_id]
        if 'largest_mass' in tc_data['tc_location'].values:
            largest_mass_tc = tc_id
            break

    if largest_mass_tc is None:
        # Fallback to TC1 if no largest_mass
        largest_mass_tc = tc_ids[0]

    else:

        }

q1_result = {

    "violating_runs": sorted(violating_runs),
    "max_ramp_by_run": {k: max_ramp_by_run[k] for k in sorted(max_ramp_by_run.keys())}
}

with open('/app/output/q01.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q1_result, f, indent=2)

print(f"Q1: Found {len(violating_runs)} violating runs")

# QUESTION 2: Time Above Liquidus (TAL) for each run
# =============================================================================
print("Processing Question 2...")

def calculate_tal(df, liquidus_temp):
    """Calculate time above liquidus temperature."""
    df = df.sort_values('time_s')
    temps = df['temp_c'].values
    times = df['time_s'].values

    tal_seconds = 0
    for i in range(1, len(temps)):
        if temps[i-1] >= liquidus_temp or temps[i] >= liquidus_temp:
            # Count this interval if either endpoint is above liquidus
            dt = times[i] - times[i-1]
            tal_seconds += dt

    # More precise: only count time actually above liquidus
    tal_seconds = 0
    for i in range(1, len(temps)):
        dt = times[i] - times[i-1]
        # If both points above liquidus, count full interval
        if temps[i-1] >= liquidus_temp and temps[i] >= liquidus_temp:
            tal_seconds += dt
        # If crossing threshold, count partial
        elif temps[i-1] >= liquidus_temp or temps[i] >= liquidus_temp:
            tal_seconds += dt / 2  # Approximate

    return tal_seconds

for run_id in sorted(all_runs):

    if load_factor > 0:

    else:

run_yields = {}

    # Skip if no runs
    if family_runs.empty:
        continue

    # Check compliance for each run based on Q1-Q4 results
    def get_run_score(run_id):
        """Calculate a score for each run based on quality and efficiency."""
        run_data = family_runs[family_runs['run_id'] == run_id].iloc[0]

        # Quality: higher yield is better
        yield_pct = run_yields.get(run_id, 0)

        # Efficiency: higher boards_per_min is better
        boards_per_min = run_data['boards_per_min']

        # Check if run is compliant (from Q1-Q4)
        is_violating_ramp = run_id in violating_runs
        is_failing_peak = run_id in failing_runs

        q2_run = next((r for r in q2_results if r['run_id'] == run_id), None)
        is_tal_non_compliant = q2_run and q2_run['status'] == 'non-compliant'

        q4_run = next((r for r in q4_results if r['run_id'] == run_id), None)
        is_speed_non_compliant = q4_run and not q4_run['meets']

        # Penalize non-compliant runs
        compliance_penalty = 0
        if is_violating_ramp:
            compliance_penalty += 100
        if is_failing_peak:
            compliance_penalty += 100
        if is_tal_non_compliant:
            compliance_penalty += 50
        if is_speed_non_compliant:
            compliance_penalty += 25

        # Score: yield is primary, boards_per_min is secondary
        # Higher score is better
        score = yield_pct - compliance_penalty + boards_per_min * 0.1

        return score

    # Calculate scores for all runs
    run_scores = [(run_id, get_run_score(run_id)) for run_id in family_runs['run_id']]
    run_scores.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))  # Sort by score desc, then run_id asc

    best_run = run_scores[0][0]
    runner_ups = [r[0] for r in run_scores[1:]]

    q5_results.append({
        "board_family": board_family,
        "best_run_id": best_run,
        "runner_up_run_ids": sorted(runner_ups)
    })

with open('/app/output/q05.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(q5_results, f, indent=2)

print(f"Q5: Processed {len(q5_results)} board families")

print("\nAll questions processed successfully!")

# =============================================================================

import json
import numpy as np

class NpEncoder(json.JSONEncoder):
    def default(self, obj):
        if isinstance(obj, np.integer):

        if isinstance(obj, np.floating):
            return float(obj)
        if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray):
            return obj.tolist()
        return super(NpEncoder, self).default(obj)

tc_df = pd.read_csv('/app/data/thermocouples.csv')

defects_df = pd.read_csv('/app/data/test_defects.csv')

TAL_MIN_S = 30
TAL_MAX_S = 60

# =============================================================================

def calculate_ramp_rates(df):

    df = df.sort_values('time_s')
    temps = df['temp_c'].values
    times = df['time_s'].values

    ramp_rates = []
    for i in range(1, len(temps)):
        dt = times[i] - times[i-1]
        if dt > 0:
            dtemp = temps[i] - temps[i-1]
            ramp_rate = dtemp / dt
            # Only consider preheat zone (100-150°C)
            # We look at the temperature at the start of the interval
            if PREHEAT_MIN_C <= temps[i-1] <= PREHEAT_MAX_C:

    return ramp_rates

tc_runs = tc_df['run_id'].unique()

# Handbook says to use the "largest mass" thermocouple for measuring thermal mass differential
# The largest_mass thermocouple is the most representative for preheat ramp rate

max_ramp_by_run = {}

    if load_factor > 0:
